1:
Every soul is read as every person, the point being that nobody is exempt. Ellicott and Robertson both call it a Hebraism, Ellicott adding a stress on man as a conscious being capable of moral relations. Chrysostom presses the scope hardest: these regulations are for all, even priests and monks, not men of secular occupations only — if thou be an Apostle even, or an Evangelist, or a Prophet, or anything whatsoever. Theodoret says the same: whether a man be priest, bishop, or monastic, let him be subject. Henry turns it into controversy: every soul means every person, not excluding the clergy, however the church of Rome may exempt them and place them above the civil powers, making the greatest princes subject to the pope. Calvin takes soul to bear on the manner rather than the extent, as showing the obedience should be sincere and genuine, not feigned.

Three of them, from three schools, converge on one distinction: what is ordained is the office, not the officer. Theodoret puts it most exactly: it is the ordinance of ruling and being ruled that the Apostle derives from the providence of God, not so much the elevation of this or that individual; not the sway of the unjust but the constitution of the office itself is of God’s appointment. Ellicott finds it strange that the Apostle seems to go out of his way to include even usurped and tyrannical power, and resolves it the same way: he speaks of the magistracy in its abstract form, the magistrate as magistrate, not as just or unjust. Robertson states the negative side flatly: Paul is not arguing for the divine right of kings or for any special form of government, but for government and order; nor does he here oppose revolution for a change of government, though he opposes all lawlessness, God being author of order, not anarchy. Henry had noticed that the duty is expressed not by the persons in power but by the place of power itself, so that however wicked the persons, the just power they hold must be obeyed.

The limit is stated as plainly as the duty. Theodoret attaches it to the command: let him be subject, if it be consistent with duty to God, for any opposition to the divine laws leaves us not the power of obeying our rulers. Barnes carries the same reservation, that the laws are implied not to violate the rights of conscience or oppose the laws of God. Henry marks the same ground from the other side: our consciences are not subject to the will of any man, since it is God’s prerogative to make laws that bind conscience. Wesley presses the positive claim, that the powers are God’s deputies or vicegerents, their authority being in effect his, and so demanding conscientious obedience.

Why the subject arises is explained historically. Gill observes that the previous chapter contains the apostle’s Christian Ethics and this his Christian Politics, the primitive saints lying under the imputation of being seditious persons and enemies to the commonwealth. Clarke dates the letter about the year 58, four or five years after the edict banishing the Jews from Rome, which a Roman historian ascribes to their continual disturbances under one Christus; Christians were then generally confounded with Jews. Barnes sets out the difficulty in principle: Christians professed supreme allegiance to Christ as Lawgiver and Judge, while the kingdoms were pagan and many of their monarchs blood-stained and oppressive; the question could not long be avoided, since the hands of those magistrates were soon to be raised against Christians in the fiery scenes of persecution. On the condemnation threatened, Ellicott takes it for the sentence passed by the judge as God’s representative, Clarke for the verdict of the constitution the seditious pretend to improve, Calvin for the punishment inflicted by God, and Wesley will have both, from the magistrate and from God.
3:
That rulers are no terror to good works is qualified before it is accepted. Barnes concedes the objection: it may not be universally true, many rulers having persecuted the good; but it is generally true that the virtuous have nothing to fear from the laws, and universally true that their appointment was designed not to oppress the good but to punish evil. Robertson makes the same reservation with a date attached: Paul does not approve all that rulers do, but speaks of the ideal before them — and Nero was Emperor. Ellicott adds why the ideal holds in law: human law takes account only of what is done, not the intention. Theodoret states the rule flatly, that they chastise those who live in wickedness; Wesley distinguishes two fears, one preceding evil actions and deterring from them, which should remain, and one following them, from which the well-doing are free.

Clarke turns the verse into a standard for the ruler, not the subject. Power is entrusted to the magistrate not for the terror of the upright but to overawe the wicked, for the community and not his own aggrandisement; if he uses it to rob and oppress his subjects he is not only a bad man but a bad prince, infringing the principles of law and equity. Should he persecute loyal subjects on a religious account, they must count him not a blessing but a plague — and yet, Clarke adds, even then the truly pious will not feel that this justifies rebellion. Calvin argues the duty from utility: the Lord has designed thus to provide for the tranquillity of the good and restrain the wicked, and unless their fury be resisted all would come to confusion, so we ought to observe this remedy unless we wish to avow ourselves public enemies of the human race. Wanting to be rid of this fear, he adds, is an implied proof of an evil conscience.

Conscience is the second and better motive. Barnes gives the two reasons already laid down, that government was appointed by God and violation exposes to punishment. Clarke sorts them: dread of punishment weighs with the ungodly, a good conscience with everyone who fears God. Theodoret takes wrath for punishment and binds both grounds together. Calvin presses furthest: though the magistrate were disarmed, so that we could despise him with impunity, the thing ought no more be attempted than if punishment hung over us, since it belongs to no private individual to take away authority from one the Lord has set over us. He then closes the door the other way: the whole discourse concerns civil government, so those who would rule consciences establish nothing from it.

Tribute follows from the office. Gill makes payment a case of conscience, not prudence: defrauding the magistrate injures the whole body politic, so such a man forfeits his claim to protection. Clarke allows nothing more reasonable than moderate taxation, but denies any insinuation in the apostle’s words on behalf of oppressive taxation for unnecessary wars or the pensioning of corrupt men; and by God’s ministers, he insists, are meant civil officers, not ministers of religion. Ellicott observes that the two words rendered minister differ, one giving us deacon and the other liturgy; Robertson notes that paying taxes recognises authority, and that paying debts needs emphasis still, even among ministers. On the dues Clarke distinguishes tribute, on persons and estates, from custom, laid on goods; Ellicott separates officers who can only claim respect from those with power to punish. Henry widens it past the magistrate: to be just is to give everybody his own, rendering to God his due first, then to families, the commonwealth, the church and the poor, not tarrying till the law compels. The catena sets beside these verses a passage of Cyril of Jerusalem on rejoicing because redemption has drawn nigh, which belongs to the chapter’s close.
8:
Four make the one debt that cannot be cleared the point of the verse. Ellicott sets out the transition: when you have paid all your other debts, taxes and customs and reverence, one remains unpaid, the universal debt of love, which must remain the root and spring of all your actions. Robertson puts it in a figure: the debt can never be paid off, but we should keep the interest paid up. Theodoret turns the paradox over: not that we are not to pay the debt of love, which we ought to discharge before anything else, but that we increase it by paying, such discharge augmenting the debt by making love the warmer. Wesley calls it an eternal debt never sufficiently discharged, which yet, rightly performed, discharges the rest.

Three take the debt literally too. Gill extends it to what arises from natural and civil relations, and to money borrowed or owed on contract, allowing that an honest man may be disabled from payment, but condemning those who run into debt and take no care to pay. Barnes reads it with a limitation, that we are not to be indebted so as to injure a man, and thinks the rule a remedy for bad debts, teaching industry and frugality. Henry is blunter about the conscience of it: Christians are to avoid useless expense, stand aloof from venturesome speculations, and not spend on themselves what they owe to others; many sensible of the trouble of being in debt think little of the sin of it.

Clarke marks off what is owed to whom. To the civil magistrate Christians owe subjection, reverence, obedience and tribute; to their brethren nothing but mutual love and the offices springing from it, being bound not by obedience but by love, which prevents their doing anything by which a brother may be injured. Calvin runs the connection the other way, back into the earlier verses. He reports that some take the clause as a taunt against those who would allow no law but love, and prefers to read it simply: in requiring obedience to princes the apostle requires nothing beyond what love demands, since whoever wishes the good well must wish the laws to prevail. He then draws the conclusion nobody else draws: he who introduces anarchy violates love, for what follows anarchy is the confusion of all things. Since magistrates are guardians of peace and justice, he adds, whoever desires every man’s right secured ought to defend their power, while the enemies of government show a disposition to do harm.

The list of commandments raises small questions. Gill notes that the fifth is omitted, either because urged already so far as it concerns magistrates, or because by the Jewish division it belonged to the first table; and the seventh stands before the sixth, which is of no moment, since there is no first nor last in the law. Barnes agrees that honouring parents is passed over, perhaps as not to the purpose in discoursing of love to a neighbour, and reports the clause forbidding false witness rejected by the best critics as doubtful. Cyril of Jerusalem quotes the same commandments in a history of failure: in the lifetime of the lawgiver who said thou shalt not commit adultery a man dared transgress, and the prophets sent to cure Israel could not overcome the disease. Henry states the measure of the royal law: to love a neighbour as oneself is to love him with the same sincerity, though not the same degree, and on this the golden rule is built. On the last phrase Ellicott observes that the Greek implies not merely that love helps a man to fulfil the law but that in the presence of love the law is fulfilled; Robertson calls it the filling up of the law; Calvin restricts it to the part referring to mankind, the first table not being in view.
11:
The hour is the argument. Chrysostom says the time of judgment is at the doors, and where in other letters the apostle used such words to cheer the troubled, here he uses them to rouse the sleeping: near is the Resurrection, near the awful Judgment, near the day that burneth as a furnace. Theodoret puts it shortly: this is no time for sleep but for arousing ourselves, since each day we draw nearer to the coming of the Lord. Ellicott notes that the word for time here means a definite and critical season, and takes the salvation for that participation in the kingdom which the Messiah at his coming should inaugurate. Robertson agrees, then qualifies the expectation: final salvation is meant, whether it comes by the second coming as they all hoped or by death, and either way it is true of us all. Clarke reports a paraphrase to the same effect, that the shortness of the present season should make us shake off sleep, and mentions the alternative, the nearness of deliverance from the persecutions then afflicting them.

Two work the metaphor rather than the timetable. Wesley draws it out piece by piece: this life a night, the resurrection the day, the gospel shining on the heart the dawn; we are to awake, to rise and throw away the night-clothes fit only for darkness and put on new, and, being soldiers, to arm and prepare for fight, lest sleep steal upon us again. Henry organises the figure into a Christian’s directory for his day’s work — when to awake, how to dress, how to walk, what provision to make — and reads the sleep as several at once, of sin, of carnal security, of sloth and of spiritual deadness, noting that both the wise and the foolish virgins slumbered. Calvin supplies a different image: men in public life take diligent care to commit nothing base, because if they do amiss they are exposed to many witnesses; and we, who always stand in the sight of God and of angels, and whom Christ the true sun of righteousness invites to his presence, ought to be far more careful.

On the vices the notes turn lexical. Clarke goes to the Greek lexicographers for the first pair, where rioting covered dissolute songs and banquets and drunkenness the festivals kept to the gods after sacrifice; and he objects that chambering is no legitimate English word, conveying no sense until one is forced upon it, the original meaning prostitution of every kind. Robertson observes that the first four words stand in the plural — revellings, drunkennesses and the rest — while strife and jealousy are singular. Calvin finds a pattern the others miss: there are three pairs, and in each the vice that seems to follow is placed first, revelling before the drunkenness that goes before it, chambering before the wantonness which is its source; ambition, he adds, is the fountain of envy and contention. Theodoret makes the same connection from experience: drunkenness provokes lewdness and obscene songs, being the parent of wantonness and teacher of quarrelsomeness. Barnes and Gill keep the plain sense: men do their foul deeds by night and live decently in open light, so Christians are to live as if all their conduct were seen.

Putting on Christ is explained as a known idiom. Barnes notes the phrase, harsh in English, was not unusual among Greek writers, who could speak of having put on Tarquin or Pythagoras, meaning to imbibe a man’s principles and become like him. Gill takes it first of the righteousness of Christ, the best robe and change of raiment, received by faith and pleaded daily, then of imitation, to walk as he walked. Ellicott adds the note remembered longest, that this verse, catching the eye of one famous convert, had great effect in leading to his baptism and change of life.
